subtopic_detail: Napkin eruption that involves the skin folds and has not responded to barrier and steroid
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 7 month old girl whose mother says her bottom has been raw for a fortnight and is getting worse rather than better. She has been changing the nappy more often and applying a zinc barrier cream at every change, and has used 1 per cent hydrocortisone ointment twice daily for the last five days.

The napkin area shows confluent beefy red erythema that extends deep into both inguinal creases and the natal cleft, with a scattering of small red papules and a few pustules on normal looking skin several centimetres beyond the main rash. There are no erosions, no bullae and no perianal fissures. She finished a course of amoxicillin for otitis media three weeks ago. She is afebrile, feeding well and thriving.

data_table.Examination: Confluent erythema involving both inguinal creases and the natal cleft, satellite papules and pustules on adjacent normal skin, oral cavity clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Change to a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied twice daily for a week
options.rationale: Potent steroids are avoided under an occlusive nappy because absorption is high and atrophy follows, and escalating steroid potency in an untreated candidal infection makes it worse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue the barrier preparation alone and change the nappy more frequently
options.rationale: Barrier and frequent changes are the treatment for irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the flexures because the skin there is not in contact with urine and faeces (Source: RCH Melbourne: Napkin rash).

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole as a single weight based dose with review in a week
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal therapy is reserved for extensive, recurrent or immunocompromised disease, and topical treatment clears an uncomplicated napkin candidiasis without systemic exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Apply topical mupirocin ointment three times daily for seven days to the area
options.rationale: Antibacterial treatment addresses impetiginised dermatitis with honey coloured crusting or bullae, and the pustules here sit on erythematous satellite lesions typical of yeast rather than staphylococcal infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Apply a topical imidazole antifungal cream at each nappy change with the barrier
options.rationale: Involvement of the depths of the flexures with satellite papules and pustules distinguishes candidal infection from irritant dermatitis, and a topical imidazole applied under the barrier is the treatment, particularly after a recent antibiotic course (Source: RCH Melbourne: Napkin rash).

explanation.summary: Napkin dermatitis is usually irritant in origin, caused by prolonged contact with urine and faeces under occlusion, and it characteristically affects the convex surfaces while sparing the depths of the flexures. When the rash goes into the creases, spreads beyond the nappy line as separate satellite lesions, or fails to respond to barrier treatment within a few days, secondary candidal infection is the usual explanation and recent antibiotic exposure makes it more likely. Persistent napkin eruptions that resist both barrier and antifungal treatment should prompt consideration of psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, zinc deficiency and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, the last suggested by petechiae and erosions. Low potency hydrocortisone is safe under a nappy for a short course, but potent corticosteroids are not, because occlusion greatly increases absorption. Persistent perianal fissuring or unusual bruising in the area should raise the question of non accidental injury.
key_points: Irritant dermatitis spares the flexures; candidal infection involves them.
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main rash are the diagnostic clue to yeast.
Recent antibiotic exposure substantially raises the risk of secondary candidal infection.
Only low potency corticosteroids are used under an occlusive nappy, and only briefly.
A rash resistant to both barrier and antifungal treatment needs a wider differential.
explanation.pearls: Check the mouth as well as the nappy area, since oral thrush and napkin candidiasis frequently coexist in an infant after antibiotics and treating only one end leaves a reservoir that reseeds the other.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of recurrent apnoea in a stable preterm infant
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a boy born at 28 weeks and 3 days gestation, now 11 days old and 1180 g. Nursing staff report six episodes over the last 24 hours in which he stops breathing for around 20 seconds, the heart rate falls into the 80s and the saturation dips, each recovering with gentle tactile stimulation.

The episodes began on day three and have been gradually more frequent. He is in room air with no increased work of breathing between episodes, tolerating full enteral feeds of expressed breast milk, and gaining weight. A septic screen two days ago including blood culture was negative and his C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage, his blood glucose has been consistently normal and his haemoglobin is 132 g/L. He has not yet received any respiratory stimulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute between episodes, blood pressure 54/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), blood culture no growth at 48 hours, haemoglobin 132 g/L, glucose within normal limits, cranial ultrasound no intraventricular haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin pending cultures
options.rationale: New or abruptly worsening apnoea in a preterm infant does demand a sepsis workup, but a negative screen two days ago with a normal C reactive protein and a gradual course over eight days argues against infection here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal handbook).

options.text: Commence caffeine citrate with a loading dose followed by daily maintenance
options.rationale: Caffeine is the first line respiratory stimulant for apnoea of prematurity, reducing apnoea frequency within a day and also reducing bronchopulmonary dysplasia and cerebral palsy at follow up in preterm infants (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal handbook).

options.text: Commence nasal continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cm of water pressure
options.rationale: Positive pressure is the next step when apnoea persists despite caffeine or when there is an obstructive component, and applying it to an infant comfortable in room air adds feeding and nasal trauma risk (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn).
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor and thicken feeds to treat gastro oesophageal reflux
options.rationale: Reflux has not been shown to cause apnoea of prematurity, and acid suppression in preterm infants increases necrotising enterocolitis and late onset sepsis (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn).
source_refs: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude seizures presenting as apnoea
options.rationale: Seizures can present as apnoea but are usually accompanied by other stereotyped movements or eye deviation and by a normal or rising heart rate, whereas apnoea of prematurity is accompanied by bradycardia (Source: RCH Melbourne: Neonatal handbook).

explanation.summary: Apnoea of prematurity reflects immaturity of the brainstem respiratory centre and of the chemoreceptor response to carbon dioxide, and its incidence rises steeply as gestational age falls, affecting nearly every infant born before 28 weeks. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so sepsis, anaemia, hypoglycaemia, intracranial haemorrhage, seizure, necrotising enterocolitis and temperature instability are considered whenever the pattern changes abruptly rather than evolving gradually. Bradycardia accompanying the pause distinguishes it from the tachycardia usually seen with seizure related apnoea. Caffeine is given until roughly 34 weeks postmenstrual age with a symptom free period before discharge, and it is one of the few neonatal drugs with a demonstrated benefit on long term neurodevelopmental outcome. Positive airway pressure is added when episodes continue despite caffeine, and intubation is reserved for infants whose apnoea does not respond to both.
key_points: Apnoea of prematurity is a diagnosis of exclusion; an abrupt change in pattern prompts a sepsis workup.
Caffeine citrate is first line and reduces bronchopulmonary dysplasia and cerebral palsy at follow up.
Continuous positive airway pressure is the next step when caffeine alone is insufficient.
Acid suppression for presumed reflux does not help and raises sepsis and necrotising enterocolitis risk.
Bradycardia with the pause suggests apnoea of prematurity rather than seizure.
explanation.pearls: Caffeine has a wide therapeutic index and a half life of about 100 hours in the preterm infant, so routine plasma level monitoring is unnecessary and a single loading dose covers the first several days on its own.

sources.label: Safer Care Victoria: Apnoea in the newborn
Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Imaging an infant with hip risk factors after the neonatal examination signs have disappeared
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 10 week old girl at her first specialist appointment. She was born at 39 weeks in the frank breech position by caesarean section, and her mother was treated for hip dysplasia as a baby.

Her newborn examination in hospital was documented as normal, and no imaging was arranged because no clunk was felt. Today Ortolani and Barlow tests produce no clunk on either side. There is an extra skin crease on the left thigh compared with the right, hip abduction is 70 degrees on the right and 55 degrees on the left, and with the hips and knees flexed the left knee sits slightly lower than the right. She feeds and grows normally and moves both legs.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow negative bilaterally, left hip abduction 55 degrees and right 70 degrees, asymmetric left thigh crease, left knee lower on Galeazzi testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents, since the neonatal and current examinations were both normal
options.rationale: The provocation tests lose sensitivity after about eight to twelve weeks as soft tissues tighten, so a negative examination at this age carries far less weight than the asymmetric abduction and crease (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph before the orthopaedic appointment
options.rationale: The femoral head is still largely cartilaginous at this age, so a radiograph is difficult to interpret and becomes the imaging of choice from about four to six months when ossification is established (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound and refer to a paediatric orthopaedic service
options.rationale: Ultrasound images the cartilaginous infant hip and quantifies acetabular development and femoral head coverage, and breech presentation with a first degree family history plus asymmetric abduction is precisely the combination that requires it (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Fit a Pavlik harness now and review the hip clinically in six weeks
options.rationale: Harness treatment follows an imaging diagnosis, since applying it to a normal hip carries risks of avascular necrosis and femoral nerve palsy for no benefit (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Repeat the clinical examination at six months of age and image only if abnormal
options.rationale: Waiting until six months forfeits the window in which simple harness treatment works, after which the alternative is closed or open reduction under anaesthesia (Source: RACGP: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in general practice

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip spans a spectrum from a shallow acetabulum to frank dislocation, and it is the commonest cause of hip arthritis requiring replacement in young adults when missed. Australian practice screens clinically at birth, at the six week check and at subsequent well child visits, and adds targeted ultrasound for infants with risk factors, principally breech presentation in the third trimester, a first degree family history and an abnormal or equivocal examination. Provocation tests are most informative in the first weeks and become unreliable after about three months, at which point limited abduction, asymmetric thigh creases and apparent femoral shortening become the important signs. Ultrasound is the modality until the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months, after which plain radiography takes over. Treatment before six months is usually a Pavlik harness worn for six to twelve weeks with ultrasound monitoring, and success rates fall substantially once walking has begun.
key_points: Breech presentation and a first degree family history are the two strongest risk factors.
Ortolani and Barlow tests lose sensitivity after about eight to twelve weeks.
Limited abduction, asymmetric creases and apparent femoral shortening dominate after that.
Ultrasound is the imaging modality until about four to six months, then plain radiography.
Harness treatment starts only after imaging confirms the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Asymmetric abduction with a difference of more than about 20 degrees is a stronger predictor than an asymmetric thigh crease, which occurs in a substantial minority of entirely normal infants and on its own does not justify imaging.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
RACGP: Developmental dysplasia of the hip in general practice
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Newborn hip assessment

subtopic_detail: Imaging the hip when an adolescent presents with knee pain and a limp
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12 year old boy brought by his mother with six weeks of aching in the left knee that is worse at the end of a school day. He weighs 74 kg and his body mass index sits well above the 97th centile.

He has not fallen or been tackled and the pain came on without an injury. He walks with the left foot turned outwards and swings the leg through rather than bending it normally. The left knee looks and feels the same as the right, with no effusion, no joint line tenderness, full flexion and extension and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip, the leg rotates outwards on its own and he stops you at about 60 degrees because of groin discomfort. He is afebrile and his C reactive protein is 3 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), knee examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Anteroposterior and frog leg lateral radiographs of both hips
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with referred knee pain is the classic presentation of a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, the lateral view detects early slips missed on the frontal view, and both hips are imaged because the other side slips in a substantial minority (Source: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the symptomatic left knee
options.rationale: Imaging where the pain is felt is the specific trap in this condition, since hip pathology refers to the knee through the obturator nerve and a normal knee film falsely reassures (Source: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee to assess for a meniscal tear
options.rationale: A meniscal injury would follow a twisting mechanism and produce joint line tenderness or an effusion, and none of those features is present on a normal knee examination (Source: RCH Melbourne: The limping child).

options.text: Ultrasound of both hips to look for an effusion in the joint
options.rationale: Ultrasound answers the question of effusion in suspected septic arthritis or transient synovitis, and an afebrile boy with a normal C reactive protein and a six week history does not fit either (Source: RCH Melbourne: The limping child).

options.text: No imaging, with referral to physiotherapy for anterior knee pain rehabilitation
options.rationale: Patellofemoral pain is a diagnosis of exclusion in this age group and does not explain restricted hip flexion with obligate external rotation, and continued weight bearing risks progression to an unstable slip (Source: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: A slipped upper femoral epiphysis occurs when the femoral head displaces posteriorly and inferiorly through the growth plate, typically in an overweight adolescent during the growth spurt, and it is one of the diagnoses most reliably delayed in paediatric practice. Between a fifth and a half of patients complain only of knee or thigh pain because the hip refers along the obturator nerve, so hip examination is mandatory in every adolescent with knee pain and no injury. The physical signs are loss of internal rotation and obligate external rotation as the hip is flexed. Radiographs must include a frog leg lateral view, because a mild slip can look normal on the frontal projection alone. Management is urgent non weight bearing and surgical fixation in situ, since progression from a stable to an unstable slip raises the risk of avascular necrosis from a few per cent to close to half. Endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency are considered in a child who is young, short or thin for this diagnosis.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain and no injury.
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the signature physical sign.
A frog leg lateral view is required because early slips are missed on the frontal view alone.
Image both hips, since the contralateral side slips in a substantial minority.
Make the child non weight bearing immediately, as progression to an unstable slip risks avascular necrosis.
explanation.pearls: Avascular necrosis complicates under about 5 per cent of stable slips but approaches 50 per cent once the slip becomes unstable, which is why crutches and a bed are ordered from the emergency department rather than after the orthopaedic review.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Treating a mite infestation across a household rather than the presenting child alone
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3 year old boy whose mother says he scratches himself raw every night and barely sleeps, though he seems settled during the day. The rash started about five weeks ago.

There are excoriated red papules across his trunk and limbs, and on close inspection short wavy grey lines a few millimetres long between the fingers and along both wrist creases. There are firm red nodules in both axillae. His mother says her own arms have started itching this week and his 6 year old sister has been scratching for a fortnight. He is otherwise well, afebrile, and there is no honey coloured crusting or surrounding cellulitis. He weighs 15 kg.

data_table.Examination: Burrows in the finger webs and wrist flexures, excoriated papules on the trunk and limbs, nodules in both axillae, no crusting or spreading erythema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply 5 per cent permethrin cream to the child and every household member on one day
options.rationale: Topical permethrin is the first line treatment in Australian practice, and treating the whole household simultaneously whether or not each person itches is what prevents the reinfestation cycle that follows treating the index child alone (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Apply 5 per cent permethrin cream to the child alone and review him in one week
options.rationale: Treating only the symptomatic child leaves untreated contacts who are already infested, and reinfestation follows within weeks, which is the commonest reason a course appears to have failed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Give a single weight based dose of oral ivermectin repeated after two weeks
options.rationale: Oral treatment is reserved for crusted disease, institutional outbreaks or failed topical therapy, and it is not recommended for children under 15 kg or under five years of age (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Apply undiluted 25 per cent benzyl benzoate emulsion overnight to the whole family
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is an alternative but must be diluted for young children because the undiluted preparation causes marked burning and irritant dermatitis at this age (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe a moderately potent topical corticosteroid and an oral antihistamine at night
options.rationale: Suppressing the itch without killing the mite allows the infestation to continue and to spread, though a steroid does have a place alongside treatment for the itch that persists afterwards (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Scabies is a mite infestation transmitted by prolonged skin to skin contact, and the intense nocturnal itch is a delayed hypersensitivity response that takes four to six weeks to develop on first exposure and only days on reinfestation. Burrows in the finger webs, wrist flexures, axillae, umbilicus and genitals are the diagnostic sign, and in infants and young children the palms, soles, scalp and face are also involved, so treatment in that age group covers the whole body rather than stopping at the neck. Every household member and any recent close contact is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms, and bedding and clothing from the preceding days are hot washed or sealed for a week. The itch commonly persists for two to four weeks after successful treatment and is managed with emollients, topical corticosteroid and antihistamine rather than with repeated scabicide. Crusted scabies, seen with immunosuppression or in remote community settings, carries an enormous mite burden, is highly transmissible and needs combined oral and topical therapy.
key_points: Treat every household member and close contact on the same day, whether or not they itch.
In children under two the application covers scalp, face, palms and soles as well as the body.
Wash bedding and clothing in hot water or seal it for at least a week.
Post scabetic itch lasts two to four weeks and is not a sign of treatment failure.
Oral ivermectin is reserved for crusted disease, outbreaks or failed topical therapy.
explanation.pearls: A second application of permethrin seven days after the first is standard practice because the cream is not reliably ovicidal, and eggs surviving the first treatment hatch within that week.
